## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dabbhapupphajātaka* (Ja 400) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to its commentary, the Buddha delivered the discourse while residing at Jetavana concerning the covetous monk Upananda of the Sakya clan [Fausböll 1883]. The framing verse and story recount a fable illustrating how quarreling results in mutual loss: two otters cooperatively catch a large carp (*rohitamaccha*) but quarrel over how to apportion it [Anandajoti 2010; Collins; Fausböll 1883]. They ask a passing jackal to arbitrate their dispute; the jackal acts as judge, awarding the head to one otter, the tail to the other, and taking the substantial middle portion for himself before returning to his mate, reflecting an ironic perspective on arbitration and jurisprudence [Anandajoti 2010; Collins; Fausböll 1883].
